abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most prevalent chronic liver disease worldwide, yet approved pharmacotherapies remain limited. The ovarian tumor domain-containing protein 1 (OTUD1) has been implicated in metabolic regulation, but its role in MASLD remains unclear. OTUD1 expression was significantly elevated in liver samples from patients with MASLD and in high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice, a finding further supported by two independent Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) cohorts (GSE24807 and GSE126848). Studies using systemic Otud1-knockout mice showed that Otud1 deficiency markedly alleviated insulin resistance and inflammation under HFD and high-fat, methionine-restricted, choline-deficient (HFMCD) diet conditions. To assess the hepatocyte-specific and therapeutic relevance of OTUD1, Otud1 was silenced in hepatocytes using AAV8-TBG-shOtud1, which significantly ameliorated HFMCD-induced steatohepatitis. Mechanistically, integrated interactome analyses identified heat shock protein 90α (HSP90α) as a direct substrate of OTUD1. OTUD1 bound to HSP90α and removed its K48-linked polyubiquitin chains at K283, thereby preventing its proteasomal degradation and enhancing its stability. This effect was required for OTUD1-driven lipid accumulation in hepatocytes, as the catalytically inactive OTUD1-C320S mutant failed to stabilize HSP90α or promote lipid deposition. Transcriptomic profiling further revealed that OTUD1 overexpression activated lipid metabolism and inflammatory pathways in OA/PA-treated LO2 cells. Together, these findings identify OTUD1 as a previously unrecognized driver of MASLD progression through the OTUD1-HSP90α axis and suggest that OTUD1 may serve as a potential therapeutic target for metabolic liver disease.

title: Synergistic regulation of crystal structure and surface properties by cerium doping: enhancing lithium extraction performance and stability of layered titanium-based lithium-ion sieves.
abstract: Titanium-based lithium-ion sieves (HTOs) have shown significant potential for lithium extraction from brines. However, their industrial application is severely constrained by a relatively low practical adsorption capacity and structural instability arising from metal dissolution during repeated cycling. To address these issues, large-radius cerium(Ce) was incorporated into the framework of a layered titanium-based lithium-ion sieve precursor (LTO) via a high-temperature solid-state method. This strategy achieved moderate unit cell expansion, optimization of the pore structure, and synergistic regulation of surface charge properties. Microscopic characterization and adsorption kinetics revealed that Ce doping not only widened the Li+ diffusion channels and reduced mass transfer resistance, but also increased the specific surface area and enhanced surface electronegativity, providing more active sites and a favorable interfacial exchange environment for Li+. In a simulated solution with an initial Li+ concentration of 100 mg L-1, the equilibrium adsorption capacity of HTO-Ce-1% reached 36.89 mg g-1, representing a 25.3% increase compared to pristine HTO. Furthermore, this modified material exhibited favorable Li+ sieve selectivity in simulated brines containing multiple coexisting ions. Benefiting from the improved cyclic stability conferred by Ce doping, HTO-Ce-1% suppressed the dissolution loss of Ti4+ after ten adsorption-desorption cycles, exhibiting an average dissolution rate of 0.667% and maintaining a capacity retention of 90.44%. These findings suggest that the Ce-doped lithium-ion sieve holds certain promise for the extraction and recovery of lithium from lithium-bearing brines.

title: Cryoneurolysis for Spasticity in a Pediatric Patient With Cold Urticaria Managed With Targeted Skin Warming: A Case Report.
abstract: Spasticity affects a significant portion of individuals with cerebral palsy, often progressing to contractures and neuro-orthopedic deformities if left untreated. Cryoneurolysis is an emerging, mini-invasive ultrasound-guided technique that induces secondary axonotmesis of peripheral nerves through the formation of an ice ball, shown to result in months of improved range of motion. However, cold urticaria is listed as a contraindication for this procedure because of the risk of localized or systemic anaphylaxis. We present a case of a 10-year-old girl with ataxic cerebral palsy who successfully underwent multisite cryoneurolysis. She had test-confirmed cold urticaria, requiring an epinephrine autoinjector to be kept on hand. By employing skin warming techniques and guided nerve branch targeting to attempt to keep the dermis above her critical temperature threshold, the procedure was completed without adverse events, achieving significant improvements in tone and gait. This case suggests that cryoneurolysis can be performed safely and is an effective spasticity treatment for patients with cold urticaria when appropriate thermal prophylactic measures are taken.
journal: Archives of rehabilitation research and clinical translation

title: Real-World Shelf Life of Epinephrine Auto-Injectors in Canada: Implications for Renewal Frequency and Patient Burden.
abstract: Although patients in Canada at risk of anaphylaxis are recommended to maintain access to two in-date epinephrine auto-injectors (EAIs) at all times, underuse during emergencies remains common. Multiple factors contribute to this gap, but the impact of real-world shelf life has been understudied. This study examines the remaining in-pharmacy shelf life of EAIs in Canada and considers its potential implications for patient burden, renewal frequency, and anaphylaxis preparedness. In this cross-sectional study, 50 licensed Canadian pharmacists from chain, independent, grocery/mass merchandise, and hospital pharmacies completed an online questionnaire and assessed EAI stock. Participating pharmacists verified all EAI stock on site, including batch numbers and expiry dates, and reported patient disposal practices. Of the 50 participating pharmacists, 49 reported 411 EAI devices across 98 batches. The mean in-pharmacy shelf life at dispensing was 12.8 months, with 47.4% of devices having 12 months or less remaining shelf life. Disposal practices varied and expiry was the most cited reason for disposal. Shortened in-pharmacy shelf life may increase renewal frequency, cost, waste, and the risk that patients carry expired devices or no device during anaphylaxis. Longer-shelf-life epinephrine treatment options or improved distribution chain practices may help reduce patient burden and enhance anaphylaxis preparedness in Canada.
journal: Journal of market access & health policy

title: Uncovering the influence of lyoprotection on stability of mRNA-LNPs after lyophilization and high temperature storage.
abstract: Lyophilization has the potential to enhance mRNA-LNP stability at elevated temperatures. The present study aimed to comprehensively evaluate the influence of lyoprotectants on critical quality attributes (CQAs) and function of mRNA-LNPs post-lyophilization and upon storage at 4 °C, 25 °C, and 40 °C. Twelve formulations containing sucrose, trehalose, and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) and their combinations at three total lipid-to-lyoprotectant weight ratios (1:5, 1:10, and 1:20) were studied. The CQAs of lyophilized mRNA-LNPs depended on the lyoprotectant composition and the lipid-to-lyoprotectant weight ratio, with the 1:20 ratio performing best. At this ratio, mRNA-LNPs containing sucrose, sucrose: trehalose 1:1, and sucrose: trehalose: PVP 1:1:1 showed limited change in particle size, mRNA encapsulation efficiency, and in-vitro transfection efficiency compared to other formulations. Interestingly, a lipid-to-sucrose 1:10 ratio provided stabilization of particle size and encapsulation post-lyophilization but resulted in reduced transfection efficiency relative to the 1:20 ratio. Thus, similarities in physicochemical properties did not assure equivalent biological function. After one month of storage at up to 40 °C, lyophilization with sucrose: trehalose: PVP = 1:1:1 at a 1:20 ratio enabled mRNA-LNPs to maintain particle size distribution, encapsulation efficiency, mRNA integrity, and in-vitro transfection. The enhanced stability of the formulation is likely due to its higher glass transition temperature of the lyoprotectant combination. In contrast, at 40 °C, when sucrose was used as the sole lyoprotectant it crystallized, reducing its protective effect. The results highlight a strategy for high-temperature stability of mRNA-LNPs as a reference for formulation development.
journal: Journal of controlled release : official journal of the Controlled Release Society

title: A Simple Temperature-Controlled Method for Preserving Viability in Human Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Retinal Organoids During Shipment.
abstract: Retinal organoids derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) hold significant promise as a tool for advancing our understanding of human retinal development and disease, as well as for the development of therapeutic strategies. However, research utilizing hiPSC-derived retinal organoid models has been constrained by logistical challenges. A notable issue is the increasing need for scientific collaboration, as experiments requiring coordination across multiple institutions often rely on the shipping of live tissues. Transporting retinal organoids over long distances without adequate climate control can lead to tissue degradation, which may interfere with histopathological analyses and impact the results of drug screening assays. Retinal organoids are most often shipped either without temperature regulation or with lithium-ion battery-powered ambient environment systems, which are heavily regulated by standard shipping companies, thus raising costs and introducing further logistical complications. In this study, we developed and evaluated a straightforward, cost-effective, and dependable temperature-controlled technology for shipping retinal organoids that can maintain adequate shipping temperature in colder months and decrease temperature fluctuations during shipment year-round, preserving organoid tissue structure and viability.

title: DUSP4 activates adipocyte thermogenesis via CRTC3 dephosphorylation-dependent UCP1 expression.
abstract: Obesity arises when a chronic energy surplus overwhelms the storage capacity of adipocytes and subsequently causes systemic metabolic dysfunction. Adaptive thermogenesis, primarily mediated by uncoupling protein 1 (Ucp1) in adipocytes, serves to counteract obesity by dissipating excess energy as heat. Despite extensive studies on thermogenic regulation, the phosphatases that regulate this protective metabolic pathway remain poorly understood. Here we identify dual-specificity phosphatase 4 (Dusp4) as a critical modulator of adipocyte thermogenesis via direct modulation of CREB-regulated transcription coactivator 3 (Crtc3). Dusp4-knockout mice exhibit impaired thermogenic capacity, diminished Ucp1 expression, and increased susceptibility to diet-induced obesity coupled with severe insulin resistance. Mechanistically, Dusp4 directly dephosphorylates serine residues on Crtc3, facilitating its nuclear translocation and subsequent transcriptional activation of Ucp1. Depot-targeted restoration of catalytically active Dusp4 in inguinal adipose tissue rescues local thermogenic gene expression and reinstates Crtc3 dephosphorylation-dependent Ucp1 induction in Dusp4-knockout mice. Collectively, these findings identify Dusp4 as a key upstream phosphatase orchestrating the Crtc3-Ucp1 thermogenic axis, and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for obesity-associated metabolic disorders.

title: Tumor-Intrinsic HEXB Drives Endothelial-To-Mesenchymal Transition and Confers Resistance to Anti-Angiogenic Therapy in Glioblastoma.
abstract: Although anti-angiogenic (anti-VEGF) therapy is widely used for glioblastoma (GBM), its efficacy is severely limited by acquired resistance. Here, we identify endothelial-mesenchymal transition (Endo-MT) in brain endothelial cells as the primary driver of this resistance, fundamentally modulated by hexosaminidase B (HEXB). Mechanistically, HEXB directly binds and stabilizes heat shock protein 60 (HSP60) by inhibiting its ubiquitination and degradation. This stabilization upregulates insulin-like growth factor binding protein 1 (IGFBP1), thereby promoting the Endo-MT process. Addressing its clinical relevance, the combination of a HEXB inhibitor and anti-VEGF therapy exerts potent synergistic therapeutic effects in GBM murine models. Overall, our study establishes HEXB as a key driver of Endo-MT and provides a promising dual-targeting strategy to overcome anti-VEGF resistance in GBM.

title: Triggers and Modifiers of Acute Coronary Events and Implications for Practice: An Umbrella Review.
abstract:
AIM: To synthesise evidence from systematic reviews on triggers and modifiers of acute coronary events to identify clinical implications. Triggers refer to transient exposures that may precipitate acute coronary events through several potential biological and haemodynamic mechanisms.
DESIGN: An umbrella review.
DATA SOURCES: MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, Epistemonikos, and Google Scholar were searched in May 2024, and an updated search was conducted in February 2025.
METHODS: This umbrella review was conducted following Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodological guidance. Systematic reviews assessing short-term or acute triggers and acute coronary events, including acute coronary syndrome, myocardial infarction, coronary occlusion, or spontaneous coronary artery dissection, and published in English were included. The quality of included reviews was evaluated using the JBI critical appraisal instrument.
RESULTS: Twenty-four systematic reviews examining 11 acute coronary event triggers were included. The most frequently reported triggers were air pollution (n = 8 reviews), respiratory infection (n = 6), and physical exertion (n = 4). The hazard period was primarily 0-2 h for physical exertion, sexual activity, and emotional stress, while environmental and infection-related triggers extended to 7 days for air pollution, up to 20 days for heat exposure, and 28 days for respiratory infections. Population-attributable fractions were reported for physical exertion (10.6%), emotional stress (3.9%), and anger (3%). Potential modifiers of risk identified, such as regular physical activity, beta-blocker use, and influenza vaccination, highlight opportunities for personalised prevention strategies to reduce risk when exposed to potential triggers.
CONCLUSION: These findings highlight the role of triggers in acute coronary events. Future research should prioritise translating these insights into clinical nursing practice to mitigate acute event risk.
IMPACT: Awareness of trigger-specific risks can guide nurses to deliver targeted patient education, conduct precise risk assessments, and implement exposure-management strategies, particularly for individuals at elevated cardiovascular risk.
PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: Not applicable.

title: Glycopyrronium bromide, formoterol fumarate dihydrate and their related compounds with UPLC/PDA-MS for simultaneous determination in pressurized metered-dose inhaler product.
abstract: An ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) technique with photodiode array-mass spectrometry (PDA-MS) detectors has been developed and validated for the determination of glycopyrronium bromide (GB), formoterol fumarate dihydrate (FFD) and their related substances in pressurized meter dose inhalers. This marks the first time the method has been implemented. Chromatographic analyses have been carried out on a UPLC system with a single quadrupole mass spectrometer (QDa) and a PDA detector. A C18 column has been used prior to the injection valve. The column temperature was set to 40°C. For each analysis, 1 μL of sample was injected at a flow rate of 0.1 mL/minute. The mobile phases used were A (0.5% formic acid in methanol) and B (0.5% formic acid in water). The total run time of the method was 30 minutes. The PDA detector was employed at 215 nm while the mass detector was set to extracted ion chromatography (XIC) mode. The range for detecting impurities of GB was found to be between 0.28 and 0.30 ng/mL, with a limits of 0.92-1.01 ng/mL for quantification. GB and FFD demonstrated linear accuracy. We studied the accuracy of related substances within the limit of quantification value range of corresponding impurities and up to 400% of the limit value. The method we used was linear, rapid, reproducible and accurate. Our proposed method is fast, linear, accurate and reproducible. The UPLC-MS method, which utilized QDa with XIC mode, was developed to ascertain the related substances and assay of GB and FFD.

title: Chemometric analysis and evaluation of antioxidant and antidiabetic activities of Cinnamomum keralaense Kosterm. leaf essential oil nanoemulsions.
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate chemical variations and similarities of different accessions of Cinnamomum keralaense Kosterm. leaf essential oils using multivariate analysis and to assess the antioxidant and antidiabetic activities of leaf essential oil nanoemulsions (EONEs). A heat map with hierarchical clustering showed that CK2 formed a distinct cluster, while CK1 and CK3 grouped because they shared similar minor components. Principal component analysis (PCA) indicated that PC1 (71.31%) and PC2 (28.69%) explained the total variance. The 1:2 ratio EONEs showed smaller particles and moderate stability over 60 days. CK1 showed superior DPPH (0.124 mg/mL) and ABTS (0.125 mg/mL) activities, as well as in other antioxidant assays. It also demonstrated greater glucose uptake (0.65-fold) and insulin secretion (1.44-fold) than the other two accessions. Moreover, the intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test showed that CK1 reduced the blood glucose level in Wistar rats. Overall, CK1 exhibits superior bioactivity, warranting further in vivo studies.

title: Phthalates: the interplay between diet, obesity, diabetes, and gut microbiota.
abstract: Millions of tons of plastic are produced worldwide each year. Currently, it is almost impossible to avoid plastic and exposure to its effects. There are many chemical compounds that are used in its production. Some of them, classified as plasticizers, are phthalates, which are found in food packaging, toys, and many cosmetics. They give plastics durability, flexibility, and heat resistance. Humanity is exposed to these substances primarily through ingestion, i.e., processed food and its storage, and through inhalation of polluted air. Consequently, phthalates and their metabolites can be detected in the human body. Due to their ubiquity, they pose a global threat to human health. They contribute to overweight and obesity, insulin resistance, diabetes, and disorders of the nervous and endocrine systems. The purpose of this article was to review existing research on the impact of phthalates on diet, the development of obesity, and diabetes.

title: Could Climate Change Be Silently Damaging Medicines We Keep at Home?
abstract: Climate change is increasing the likelihood of medicines being exposed to temperatures outside recommended storage conditions after dispensing. Unlike controlled pharmaceutical storage and stability testing environments, everyday settings such as homes, vehicles, bags, delivery packages, domestic refrigerators, and periods of power interruption may subject medicines to fluctuating or extreme temperatures. The clinical significance of these exposures, however, remains uncertain and is likely to vary considerably between products. This scoping review maps the available evidence on post-dispensing temperature exposure and medication stability, with particular attention to real-world storage conditions, physicochemical integrity, biological activity, potential clinical consequences, and practical strategies for reducing temperature-related risk. Evidence was considered across a range of temperature-sensitive and commonly used medicines, including insulin, refrigerated biologics, epinephrine, inhaled medicines, nitroglycerin, and oral formulations, together with studies evaluating household refrigeration, vehicle exposure, and low-resource cooling approaches. The available literature indicates that medicines may frequently encounter conditions outside labelled storage recommendations after leaving formal supply chains. Nevertheless, exposure beyond a labelled temperature range should not be interpreted automatically as loss of pharmaceutical quality or clinical effectiveness. Thermal stability varies substantially according to formulation, temperature intensity, duration of exposure, cumulative thermal history, packaging, and storage conditions. Current evidence is strongest for selected temperature-sensitive medicines but remains fragmented across many other drug classes. Overall, the literature supports a plausible climate-sensitive pathway linking increasing environmental heat with post-dispensing medication-quality risk, but evidence is currently insufficient to quantify the associated clinical burden at population level. Important priorities include characterising cumulative real-world thermal exposure, establishing clinically meaningful degradation thresholds, linking temperature histories with patient outcomes, and evaluating feasible adaptation measures. Climate-resilient medication management will require clearer storage guidance, improved patient education, practical cooling solutions, more reliable refrigeration, temperature-monitoring technologies, and stronger surveillance of medicines after dispensing.

title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome in an Elderly Woman on a Haloperidol-Lithium Combination: A Diagnostic Challenge with Complete Recovery.
abstract: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a rare but potentially fatal idiosyncratic reaction to dopamine-blocking agents, characterized by hyperthermia, generalized rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered consciousness. Its recognition is particularly difficult in elderly patients, in whom the presentation may be atypical and the differential diagnosis broad. We report a 76-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia, maintained on haloperidol and lithium for approximately 3 months, who presented with high-grade fever (39.6°C), acute alteration in sensorium, and hypertension (170/110 mmHg). Examination revealed lead-pipe rigidity, bilateral tremor, and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 10/15. An initial working diagnosis of infectious encephalitis produced a diagnostic delay of 2-3 days; lumbar puncture and blood cultures were unremarkable, and creatine kinase peaked at 4120 U/L. NMS was diagnosed using diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders, fifth edition (DSM-5) and Levenson criteria. Both offending agents were withdrawn, and the patient was managed in intensive care with intravenous hydration, active cooling, bromocriptine, and lorazepam. She achieved complete neurological recovery by day 14 and was discharged without residual deficits. This case underscores that NMS must be considered early in any older patient on dopamine antagonists presenting with fever, rigidity, and altered consciousness and that the haloperidol-lithium combination carries a specific risk even at therapeutic lithium levels.

title: Fabrication of carbon dots derived from Alangium salviifolium for the sequential sensing Ag+ and S2- and further monitoring of H2S in spoiled food.
abstract: Given the significant threat posed by heavy metals to ecological system and human health, the development of precise, portable, and on-site analytical technologies is urgently required. Herein, multifunctional carbon dots (A-CDs) derived from the traditional chinese medicine (TCM) were synthesized and exhibited optimal emission at 604 nm excited at 495 nm, with quantum yield (QY) of 18.25%. The A-CDs achieved the cascade determination of Ag+ and S2- via a subsequent "on-off-on" process with LODs of 63.7 nM and 0.98 μM, respectively. Notably, A-CDs portable platform was constructed and enabled on-site quantitative analysis with LODs of 0.83 μM and 1.19 μM, respectively. Leveraging this unique sensing performance, the A-CDs test strips were developed for visual screening of H2S during food spoilage at varying storage temperatures, allowing qualitative food freshness discrimination via naked-eye observation. The precise quantitative detection in real water and foodstuff was applied, and further verified by ICP-MS, confirmed the excellent accuracy and environmental tolerance. This work presented an intelligent strategy for designing cost-effective, high-performance multivariate probes, holding significant promise for advancing food safety and environmental monitoring.
journal: Spectrochimica acta. Part A, Molecular and biomolecular spectroscopy

title: Plant-Based Virus-like Particle (VLP) Vaccines Against Influenza and Hepatitis Viruses.
abstract: The rapid evolution of pathogens, particularly viruses, poses a continuous threat to global public health, necessitating the development of highly scalable and cost-effective vaccine platforms. Plant-based virus-like particles (VLPs) have emerged as a transformative approach in vaccinology, leveraging the innate capacity of plant systems to produce highly immunogenic, non-infectious, and structurally authentic viral mimics. VLP-based recombinant antigens contained within the plant tissues (particularly in seeds) show better stability and can be transported and stored at ambient temperatures, without the requirement of a cold chain framework, and edible vaccines offer needle-free vaccine administration. Plant-based expression systems use natural cellular structures such as plant cell walls and seed endosperms to encase antigens, functioning as a natural shield against digestion and thermal degradation. Grain host plants are inimitably adapted for prolonged storage owing to natural seed desiccation wherein recombinant antigens accumulate within vacuoles or intracellular protein bodies segregated from active degradation. By simply cultivating more plants, vaccine production can be scaled up while transient plant expression systems speed up production within a few weeks, which is critical for quick responses to emerging new disease outbreaks. By genetic modification, plants can be used to express several antigens, facilitating the development of multi-component vaccines against many diseases at a single shot. Recently, plant-derived VLP vaccines, principally targeting influenza and hepatitis viruses, have been shown to elicit robust immune responses through the expression of their surface antigens in plants such as lettuce, potato, and tobacco (Nicotiana benthamiana). Despite their potential, significant challenges persist, including the achievement of consistent dosing, the attainment of high and reproducible expression levels, and the navigation of complex regulatory frameworks for plant-derived pharmaceuticals which remain unsolved. The current review focuses on recent developments in the production of plant-based influenza and hepatitis vaccines and explores the advantages, challenges, and application of such vaccines in combating these infections.

title: Structure of Li3YCl6 and Its Effect on Lithium Ionic Conductivity.
abstract: Halide-based Li+ solid-state electrolytes have garnered renewed interest in recent years, mainly because of their significantly improved Li+ ionic conductivity and excellent stability against high-voltage cathodes. Numerous studies have reported that synthetic conditions and protocols can profoundly influence cation defect chemistry, thereby affecting Li+ mobility in these materials. Despite extensive investigations, the structures and fundamental mechanisms governing Li+ transport in these compounds remain highly debated, posing challenges for further performance optimization. In this report, we present a comprehensive structural analysis of Li3YCl6 synthesized under various conditions. Our findings reveal that the structural differences among the various forms of Li3YCl6 originate from variations in the type and length scales of Y-vacancy ordering within the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) anion framework. Our results show that samples treated at lower temperatures tend to exhibit a more uniform distribution of Y3+ and vacancies across the two different cation layers. In contrast, high-temperature treatment leads to the preferential occupation of one layer by Y3+, while vacancies dominate the other layer. This temperature-driven redistribution underlies the multiple-phase transitions observed upon heat treatment. Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations on the simulated and experimental structures suggest that the Y-vacancy uniformly distributed structure exhibits more balanced in-plane Li+ diffusion behavior; in contrast to the Y-vacancy segregated phases, where Li+ diffusion is facile in the Y-poor layer but is severely hindered in the adjacent Y-rich layer. This study resolves the longstanding controversies surrounding the structure of Li3YCl6 and highlights the importance of manipulating the cation-vacancy distribution for optimizing Li+ conductivity in hcp-based layered halide electrolytes.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: A strain-insensitive multiplexed soft microneedle patch for robust interstitial fluid biomarker monitoring.
abstract: Wearable microneedle sensors analyze biomarkers in situ from interstitial fluids (ISF), enabling minimally invasive, precise, and continuous monitoring of metabolic diseases. However, conventional designs either lack adequate conformability to skin or suffer from electrode fractures during skin penetration and body motion, leading to signal instability that undermines reliable multiparameter acquisition. Here, we present a fully integrated system with a soft microneedle sensor array featuring nano-hill topographies on strain-resilient electrodes to delocalize strain via geometric confinement. This design reduces signal variability by 14-fold compared to conventional designs, enabling stable, simultaneous in situ monitoring of multiple ISF biomarkers. It achieves clinical-grade accuracy for continuous glucose monitoring (mean absolute relative difference of 10.8%) and captures dynamic synchronized variations in glucose, local tissue pH, and temperature in a living subject in real time. The system integrates a reusable electronic module with a disposable microneedle array with a sensor footprint of just 1.8 cm2. By combining high signal stability with multiparameter synchrony in a compact form factor, this system offers a practical solution for reliable, real-time ISF analysis under dynamic in vivo conditions.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Adaptive personalization for wearable non-invasive continuous glucose sensors.
abstract: Accurate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is essential for diabetes management, yet non-invasive CGM remains challenging. Universal "one-sensor-fits-all" approaches often fail, because correlations between non-invasive physiological readouts and blood glucose (BG) are highly individualized. Here, we propose a personalized "Adaptive Non-invasive CGM" methodology, which integrates a short-term minimally invasive CGM (MI-CGM) module for measuring interstitial fluid glucose, and a long-term non-invasive CGM (NI-CGM) module based on metabolic heat conformation. During a ~2-days training, the NI-CGM learns accurate sensing from the MI-CGM via GRU-based AI model, forming patient-specific sensor. The MI-CGM is then removed, leaving only the NI-CGM for long-term monitoring. In a 5-day CGM test, the system achieved MARD ~15.6%. This method also demonstrated good reproducibility and maintained reasonable accuracy (MARD ~23.9%) during long-term interval use (>2 months). This personalized approach offers a pathway from conventional "one-sensor-fits-all" strategies toward individualized sensor development, potentially mitigating inter-patient variability and non-invasive monitoring inaccuracies.

title: What triggers intraoperative blood pressure/heart rate surges and postoperative hypertonia during unilateral biportal endoscopy?
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Unilateral biportal endoscopy (UBE) is an increasingly utilized minimally invasive technique for lumbar degenerative disease. Dural tear is a recognized complication (incidence 1.9-5.8%), typically associated with cerebrospinal fluid leakage and intracranial hypotension. However, the unique irrigation dynamics of UBE - an open two-portal system permitting high-flow continuous irrigation - may produce a distinctly different pathophysiology when an occult dural defect is present. The anesthesiology literature contains few descriptions of the acute intraoperative hemodynamic manifestations of this phenomenon.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 49-year-old woman (ASA physical status I) underwent UBE for L4-L5 and L5-S1 disc herniation under total intravenous anesthesia. The procedure was complicated by intraoperative wrong-level surgery (L4-L5 misidentified as L5-S1), necessitating complete portal withdrawal, re-localization, and re-establishment of the surgical field, which prolonged the operation to 4 h 23 min with a cumulative irrigation volume of 51,000 mL. Approximately 2.5 h after incision, progressive, treatment-refractory tachycardia (70 → 117 beats/min) and hypertension (up to 183/102 mmHg) developed; esmolol and urapidil produced minimal antihypertensive effect despite concurrent augmentation of anesthetic depth. On postoperative review, the scrub nurse recalled observing a suspected dural tear approximately 10 min before the hemodynamic escalation, which had not been communicated intraoperatively. Following extubation, the patient exhibited impaired consciousness, persistent tachypnea (40-50 breaths/min), and generalized hypertonia with decerebrate posturing. Multidisciplinary evaluation excluded epileptic seizure, metabolic encephalopathy, malignant hyperthermia, and intraoperative awareness. Suspected acute intracranial hypertension secondary to massive irrigation fluid entry into the subarachnoid space via the unrecognized dural defect was considered the most likely diagnosis. The patient was reintubated and managed in the intensive care unit with osmotic diuresis (furosemide, mannitol), corticosteroids, and sedation. Consciousness recovered the following morning, limb hypertonia resolved by postoperative day 11, and the patient was discharged on day 14 without neurological deficit.
CONCLUSIONS: This case suggests that an occult dural tear during UBE with large-volume irrigation may produce a paradoxical hemodynamic profile of progressive, therapy-resistant hypertension and tachycardia - contrasting with the bradycardia and hypotension classically associated with intracranial hypotension from cerebrospinal fluid leaks. The triad of (i) progressive, treatment-refractory hypertension and tachycardia, (ii) prolonged UBE duration (> 2 h), and (iii) large-volume irrigation (> 20 L) may represent a high-risk pattern warranting immediate intraoperative communication between anesthesia and surgical teams and consideration of intracranial pressure-directed interventions. This observation is hypothesis-generating and requires validation in larger studies.

title: Container-closure Performance of an Airless Calibrated Pump for Compounded Topical Semisolids: Dispensed-mass Reproducibility, Barrier Properties, and Compatibility.
abstract: Primary packaging can be a critical determinant of performance for semisolid drug products, particularly when the dose is delivered by a metered device. This study evaluated an airless, pouch-based metered-dose dispenser (Topi-pump™) as a container-closure and dose-delivery system for topical semisolids, focusing on (i) packaging quality attributes, (ii) delivered-dose reproducibility, and (iii) compatibility during in-use/accelerated conditions. Packaging performance was assessed by UV-Vis light transmission (opacity), aqueous extractables screening by UV-Vis, and particulate contamination testing. Dose delivery was benchmarked against two comparable calibrated airless dispensers by quantifying the dispensed mass of semisolid vehicles under predefined handling conditions (orientation and temperature) over 10 days. The schedule comprised 40 recorded actuations per dispenser and did not extend to container exhaustion, so terminal-dose behavior was not characterized. Dispensed mass was evaluated against a 0.5 g ± 5% criterion. Compatibility was examined using model semisolids containing representative steroidal drug substances, compounded in multiple cream bases, under accelerated storage conditions, supported by microbiological testing guided by USP <61>/<62> and acceptance criteria from USP <1111>. The dispenser met predefined packaging criteria, showing low extractables (0.0050 AU; limit =0.20 AU), low particulate burden (largest particle 67 µm; criterion =100 µm), and low light transmission (opacity 0.15%; criterion =1.0%). In the pooled screening across all vehicles and operating conditions, the Topi-pump™ dispenser showed a mean dispensed mass closest to the nominal target and the lowest overall variability by coefficient of variation (screening CV 9.5% vs 18.6-21.2% for comparators), although pooled interquartile ranges were comparable for Topi-pump™ and Pump A, suggesting that the difference reflected observations outside the central portion of the distributions rather than central dispersion. Condition-level conformity and precision were subsequently evaluated within Pentravan® as a single fixed reference matrix, with apparent viscosity considered as part of the formulation context.with apparent viscosity considered as part of the formulation context. In the preliminary vehicle-level screening, using combined data from all three dispensing systems and all evaluated temperature-orientation conditions, observed conformity was 61.4% for Pentravan®, 46.2% for Fitalite™ (Phytobase™), 39.4% for HRT Heavy™, and 7.7% for Salt Stable™ LS Advanced. These proportions pool three devices, three temperatures and three orientations against a ±5% band, and in the most viscous vehicle they reflect a systematic offset rather than erratic delivery: in Salt Stable™ LS Advanced (96.4 Pa·s at 20 °C), Topi-pump™ delivered a median of 0.450 g per actuation with a robust coefficient of variation of 6.7%, comparable to its precision in the other vehicles evaluated, and conformity in that matrix reached 98.1% against the 75-125% individual-dose interval applied in earlier work. Drug assay remained within 90-110% of the label claim throughout the study period, with TAMC/TYMC below the reporting limit (<10 CFU/g) and the specified pathogens absent. Across the tested conditions, the airless metered-dose pouch system met the predefined container-closure acceptance criteria. It showed the lowest conventional coefficient of variation in the pooled screening and low within-condition variability in the focused Pentravan® analysis, indicating suitable performance as a delivery platform for compounded topical semisolids under these conditions.

title: Pharmacophore-based construction of spiro[indoline-3,4'-piperidine] ureas as dual-target MOR/TRPV1 lead agents for pain.
abstract: Chronic pain remains a severe clinical challenge. Conventional μ-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists produce robust analgesia but trigger severe adverse effects including analgesic tolerance and physical dependence, while single-target TRPV1 antagonists cause hyperthermia, restricting their clinical translation. Functional crosstalk between MOR and TRPV1 in pain signaling provides a rational basis for developing dual-target ligands combining MOR agonism and TRPV1 antagonism to achieve improved analgesic effects via dual-pathway regulation and mitigate single-target liabilities. Herein, we rationally designed two series of spiro[indoline-3,4'-piperidine] urea derivatives by fusing the core pharmacophores of classic TRPV1 antagonists and fentanyl-type MOR agonists, and systematically investigated their structure-activity relationships (SAR). Among all synthesized derivatives, compound 8m exhibited ideal dual-target bioactivity, with potent TRPV1 antagonism (hTRPV1 IC50 = 23 nM) and MOR agonism (EC50 = 63 nM, Emax = 94%). In vivo experiments showed that compound 8m produced dose-dependent analgesia in formalin and capsaicin-induced pain models via dual-pathway regulation. Unlike the TRPV1 antagonist BCTC, 8m did not elicit obvious hyperthermia in mice. Moreover, repeated administration of 8m hardly induced analgesic tolerance compared with morphine. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations suggested that 8m could stably bind to the pockets of both receptors through hydrogen bonds, halogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions, and maintain the rational conformational dynamics of receptor proteins. This work provides a promising spirocyclic lead compound and a feasible dual-target design strategy to mitigate partial single-target related adverse liabilities for chronic pain analgesic development.

title: Propranolol disrupts fear-induced persistent cocaine place preference and unmasks an aversion component.
abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and cocaine use disorder frequently co-occur, but how traumatic memories influence drug-associated behavior during drug withdrawal is unclear. We combined traumatic-like conditioned fear memory recall (FR) with cocaine-induced conditioned place preference (CPP) in male mice, and tested preference repeatedly during withdrawal, with or without prior FR sessions. The effects of the β-adrenergic antagonist propranolol and the CRF-R1 antagonist antalarmin administered before each FR and before fear extinction were also tested. Progressive extinction of CPP occurred along repeated testing sessions in the control condition. In contrast, repeated FRs maintained a stable, persistent preference for the cocaine-associated compartment, accompanied by an increased compulsive-like behavior in the marble burying test, hyperthermia and elevated corticosterone plasma levels. Antalarmin did not prevent the FR-induced persistence of CPP. Cluster analysis revealed instead that propranolol split animals into two subgroups: one subgroup that progressively lost preference and developed even an apparent conditioned place aversion to the cocaine-associated compartment, and another subgroup that maintained and incubated CPP. The divergence toward place aversion was somehow associated with increased conditioned freezing during FRs. Subsequent fear extinction reduced preferences in both propranolol subgroups, indicating a shared dependence on ongoing fear memory engagement. Our findings identify fear memory reactivations as an active regulator of drug-associated motivational states during withdrawal, with a noradrenergic mechanism as a proximal mediator, suggesting that β-adrenergic blockade combined with exposure-based extinction may benefit comorbid PTSD and cocaine use disorder.

title: From cold chain to home care: emerging pharmaceutical challenges in monoclonal antibody therapy.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are increasingly shifting from hospital intravenous infusion to subcutaneous self-administration at home, exposing fragile glycoproteins to thermal excursions, mechanical stress, and mishandling. These vulnerabilities are well documented in vitro and in preclinical models; however, their causal link to clinical treatment failure in home settings has not yet been established through prospective interventional or epidemiological studies.
AREAS COVERED: This review examines the pharmaceutical challenges across the mAb lifecycle: degradation mechanisms, formulation strategies for high-concentration subcutaneous products (excipients, lyophilization, hyaluronidase-facilitated delivery), cold-chain vulnerabilities from manufacture to home storage, comparative analysis of intravenous versus subcutaneous administration, home-based practice challenges, and emerging technologies including IoT monitoring, smart packaging, and wearable injectors. Literature from pharmaceutical sciences, cold-chain engineering, device technology, and clinical practice (1974-2026) was synthesized.
EXPERT OPINION: Ensuring mAb stability outside institutional walls requires an integrated four-pillar framework: mechanism-based formulation design, intelligent supply chain technologies, human-centered device engineering, and comprehensive patient education with digitally enabled professional support. While degradation mechanisms are well characterized, their translation into clinical outcomes in decentralized care remains an open research question. Future efforts should focus on thermostable formulations, validated temperature monitoring, intuitive delivery devices, and continuous care frameworks extending pharmaceutical expertise into patients' homes.

title: The WD40 domain of autophagy protein ATG-16.2 is required for lysosomal regulation and longevity in germline-less C. elegans.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Autophagy is a conserved cellular recycling pathway linked to longevity and regulated by autophagy-related (ATG) protein. Many of these proteins serve a key function in ATG8 lipidation onto autophagosomal membranes, a step that precedes subsequent lysosomal degradation. Recently, mammalian ATG16L1, a member of ATG8 lipidation machinery, have been shown to also direct ATG8 lipidation onto other membranes via its C-terminal WD40 domain in acutely stressed cells. However, whether such non-canonical functions of the ATG16L1 WD40 domain influence longevity remain largely unknown. Here, we endogenously deleted the WD40 domain of atg-16.2 , the C. elegans ortholog of ATG16L1 , and examined autophagy, healthspan and longevity. The ATG-16.2 WD40 domain was dispensable for healthspan measures and for ATG8 lipidation in whole animals and neurons but was required for autophagic flux across all major tissues examined. Notably, the ATG-16.2 WD40 domain was also critical in limiting lysosomal membrane damage after acute heat stress. Because long-lived C. elegans mutants are typically heat resistant, we asked whether this lysosomal function supported their thermotolerance and found the WD40 domain to be selectively required for thermotolerance induced by germline removal, but not by reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling or dietary restriction. In germline-less animals, loss of the ATG-16.2 WD40 domain reduced nuclear TFEB/HLH-30, reduced neuronal autophagic degradation, altered neuronal lysosomal pH, and sensitized animals to heat-induced lysosomal damage. Collectively, these findings establish the ATG16 WD40 domain as a regulator of autophagic degradation and lysosomal integrity in vivo, and show that this role is associated with longevity in a pathway-selective manner.
HIGHLIGHTS: The ATG-16.2 WD40 domain is dispensable for C. elegans healthspan but required for autophagic degradation in vivo The WD40 domain limits lysosomal membrane damage after acute heat stress in vivo The WD40 domain is selectively required for thermotolerance and longevity induced by germline removal ( glp-1/NotchR mutation) Elevated neuronal lysosomal pH in germline-less animals requires the WD40 domain.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology

title: In vitro Evaluation of the Physicochemical Stability of Multi-Drug Y-Site Admixtures Using Dynamic Monitoring and Chemometrics.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Concurrent continuous infusions of propofol, midazolam, insulin, dexmedetomidine, and morphine are commonly used in ICU for sedation, analgesia, and glycemic control. However, physicochemical compatibility data for Y-site administration are lacking, leading to risky empirical practice. This study evaluated their physicochemical stability to guide safe infusion.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Twenty-six admixtures were prepared at clinical concentrations and stored at room temperature. Samples were analyzed at 0, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h for appearance, pH, osmolality, subvisible particles, mean droplet diameter (MDD), polydispersity index (PDI), zeta potential, microscopic aggregation, and drug content by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Principal component analysis (PCA), hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA), Spearman correlation, and orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were performed to explore stability patterns and key discriminating variables.
RESULTS: No obvious alterations in appearance, pH, or osmolality were observed over 24 h. In propofol-free admixtures, subvisible particles met pharmacopeial limits. In propofol-containing admixtures, MDD (95.6-124.3 nm) and PDI (0.338-0.469) remained acceptable, whereas zeta potential ranged from -12.50 to 6.14 mV. Microscopic aggregation was observed in seven propofol-containing admixtures. HPLC showed that all drugs retained >90% of their initial concentrations. OPLS-DA identified four independent variables with VIP values greater than 1 (R2 Y=0.71, Q2=0.689), and permutation tests confirmed no overfitting.
CONCLUSION: Under the conditions studied, seven propofol-containing admixtures showed aggregation, while the other 19 remained stable for 24 h. Chemometric analysis supported the stability classification and indicated that drug composition, pH and zeta potential were key contributors to emulsion aggregation.

title: Management of vaccine cold chain equipment in the Ethiopian immunization supply chain system: evidence from the Ethiopian national immunization program evaluation.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: There is insufficient evidence on the current condition of vaccine cold chain equipment (CCE) in Ethiopia. This study is aimed to assess the status of the CCE of the Ethiopian immunization supply chain system and generate evidence to inform policymakers and donors for effective planning and decision-making.
METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted across nine regions in Ethiopia using the World Health Organization Expanded Program of Immunization review guide and the effective vaccine management 2.0 tool. Data were collected through direct observation and face-to-face interviews using the effective vaccine management assessor mobile app, assessing vaccine storage capacity, including CCE type, brand, and model, at one Ethiopian Pharmaceuticals Supply Service (EPSS) center and 15 hubs, and 286 lower distribution (LD), or service provision (SP) sites (a total of 302 immunization supply chain sites).
RESULTS: All EPSS hubs use passive storage devices and have refrigeration and/or freezer units. A total of 425 refrigerators and/or freezers were found at LD and SP levels, including 335 regular refrigerators, 17 freezers, and 73 combined units (refrigerators and freezers); 45 facilities (15.7%) reported having at least one non-functional refrigerator; 47 (16.5%) reported having at least one refrigerator that was working but in need of repair; and the remaining 194 (67.8%) reported that all their refrigerators were working well. During the survey, 235 of these refrigerators had a functioning 30-day temperature record system, 397 refrigerators were in good functional status with respect to temperature control, and 40 refrigerators/freezers were equipped with a computerized temperature-monitoring system. The total positive-temperature (2-8°c)vaccine storage capacity was 440,768 l at the central hub and 51,953 (38,666) l (mean, SD) at the sub-central hubs. The total negative-temperature (-25 to -15°c) vaccine storage capacity was 40,000 l at the central hub and 1980 (3504) l (mean, SD) at the sub-central hubs. At the LD and SP levels, the overall total positive-temperature (2-8°c) vaccine storage capacity averaged 1562.0 l (SD 12,062.1; median 37.5, interquartile range 140.0). The total negative-temperature (-25 to -15°c) vaccine storage capacity averaged 490.4 l (SD 5895.8), the total cool pack storage capacity averaged 687.8 l (SD 8188.5), and the total coolant pack storage capacity (cool pack and ice pack combined) averaged 826.9 l (SD 9627.5). The total insulated container capacity averaged 22.2 l (SD 43.5; median 7.8, interquartile range 25.6) across all facilities at the LD and SP levels. The EPSS center and 13 hubs have conducted preventive maintenance and repaired refrigerators in the past year. Most institutions (82.95%) at the LD and SP levels lack a documented preventive maintenance schedule. Only 20% of institutions maintain records of preventive maintenance.
CONCLUSION: Improving cold chain management through better temperature-monitoring, increased refrigeration, and enhanced transportation is essential to ensure vaccine potency and reduce wastage.

title: Recurrent Unexplained Fever and Suspected Promazine Toxicity: Why Probable Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome Was Left Undiagnosed in a Healthcare Worker.
abstract: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a potentially fatal adverse reaction to dopamine-antagonist medication that can resemble sepsis. A 51-year-old woman working in healthcare experienced recurrent episodes of fever, confusion and muscle rigidity, with six hospital presentations over approximately 10 months. Her prescribed medicines included promazine and amitriptyline. During an earlier severe admission, she developed hyperthermia, agitation, shock, and a creatine kinase concentration of 7272 U/L, requiring intensive care. Investigations did not identify a unifying diagnosis. During the most recent admission, review of previous records and a non-judgemental discussion elicited possible use of additional medication for sleep and neuropathic pain, although the preparation and quantity remained unclear. Six months' supply of promazine had been approved and dispensed within the preceding three months, supporting increased access without establishing the amount ingested. The clinical pattern supported a working diagnosis of probable promazine-associated NMS, with possible concomitant amitriptyline toxicity. Promazine was discontinued three days after admission. At follow-up approximately six months later, the patient remained off promazine and reported sustained symptom resolution and no further hospital attendances. This case highlights the importance of considering NMS in unexplained fever during antipsychotic treatment, conducting repeated medication reviews, and asking sensitive questions, regardless of a patient's professional healthcare background.

title: Heat-resistant collagen gel alleviates obesity through glycine release and gut microbiota remodeling.
abstract: Collagen-derived foods have emerged as promising nutritional interventions for obesity and related metabolic disorders. However, their application is limited by poor thermal stability, and the mechanisms underlying their metabolic benefits remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the anti-obesity effects and underlying mechanisms of a heat-resistant collagen gel (HHG) in high-fat diet-induced obese mice. The investigation comprehensively assessed how HHG influences obesity-related parameters and the biological mechanisms involved in mice fed a high-fat diet. Findings from the study indicated that HHG markedly decreased body weight gain in obese mice. Additionally, it enhanced glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity, lowered serum TG and T-CHO concentrations, and diminished hepatic lipid deposition. The mechanism of action can be further broken down into two aspects. First, after HHG is digested, small molecules (such as glycine) are absorbed into the bloodstream via the small intestine. By increasing serum and hepatic glycine levels, this process promotes the expression of Glutathione Synthetase (Gss) and Glutathione Reductase (Gsr), enhances the liver's antioxidant capacity, and suppresses systemic inflammatory responses. Second, after HHG digestion, large peptides that are not absorbed by the small intestine enter the large intestine. There, they significantly modulate the gut microbiota, increasing α-diversity. They also enrich bacterial genera positively correlated with metabolic health, including Alistipes and Odoribacter. In summary, HHG effectively improves obesity and related metabolic disorders. It does so by promoting glutathione synthesis, alleviating systemic inflammation, and regulating gut microbiota. This provides a theoretical basis for developing collagen-based foods.

title: Anticholinergic Agents
abstract: Anticholinergics are agents that decrease or block the actions of acetylcholine on its parasympathetic nervous system receptors on smooth muscle cells, glands and the central nervous system. Cholinergic receptors are usually categorized as nicotinic or muscarinic. Anticholinergics often demonstrate differential antagonism for different receptors types and subtypes, accounting in part for their variety of actions and clinical usefulness for different conditions. The anticholinergics in clinical use include natural, semisynthetic and synthetic compounds that demonstrate a multitude of actions on smooth muscle cells and the parasympathetic nervous system. Anticholinergics have antisecretory activities and decrease nasal and bronchial secretions, salivation, lacrimation, sweating and gastric acid production, and can be used to decrease secretions in allergic and inflammatory diseases. Anticholinergics relax smooth muscle in the gastrointestinal tract, bladder and lung and can be used for gastrointestinal, urological or respiratory conditions associated with spasm and dysmotility. Some anticholinergics have antiemetic properties and are used to prevent nausea and vomiting from motion sickness or during the perioperative period. Anticholinergics increase heart rate and can be used to treat bradycardia. They are also used to reverse cholinergic overstimulation caused by cholinesterase inhibitors and neuromuscular blockers in anesthesia. The common side effects of anticholinergic agents are largely those of parasympathetic inhibition and include dryness of the mouth and eyes, decreased sweating and hyperthermia, headache, visual blurring, constipation, urinary retention, impotence, tachycardia and palpitations, anxiety, restlessness and in some instances agitation and delusions. Anticholinergics rarely cause liver injury. Their relative safety probably relates to their use in low doses for short periods of time only. Most anticholinergics are metabolized in the liver via the cytochrome P450 system.

title: Physiology, Anticholinergic Reaction
abstract: Acetylcholine (ACh) is a neurotransmitter that acts on the central nervous system (CNS), the autonomic nervous system (ANS), and at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). Generally, ACh receptors at the NMJ are nicotinic type while in the CNS and ANS they are usually muscarinic type. As a reminder, these receptors are functionally and structurally different; nicotinic ACh receptors are ligand-gated ion channels, whereas muscarinic ACh receptors are G-protein coupled receptors. Processes that enhance ACh function are termed “cholinergic” while processes that inhibit the action of ACh at its receptors are termed “anticholinergic.” Anticholinergic effects are most commonly the result of medication. These medications should be more appropriately termed "antimuscarinics," as they usually block muscarinic but not nicotinic receptors. At least 600 drugs/medicinal products are recognized to have anticholinergic activity, and the most common of these are responsible for a significant amount of poisoning admissions. Many also contribute to the development of an anticholinergic reaction: a constellation of symptoms resulting from the antagonism of muscarinic receptors throughout the body. The features of the anticholinergic reaction are deducible from an understanding of the normal function of muscarinic receptors at various organs, and the following mnemonic summarizes these effects: Mad as a hatter (delirium). Blind as a bat (ocular symptoms). Dry as a bone (anhidrosis/dry mouth/dry skin). Hot as a hare (fever). Bloated as a toad (constipation). The heart runs alone (tachycardia). Full as a flask (urinary retention). Red as a beet (cutaneous vasodilation). Clinically the most significant feature is delirium, particularly in the elderly, who are most likely to be affected by the anticholinergic reaction.

title: PTS-Related Tetrahydrobiopterin Deficiency (PTPSD)
abstract: Clinical characteristicsPTS-related tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency (PTPSD) results in a lack of tetrahydropterin, an important cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), tyrosine hydroxylase, and tryptophan hydroxylase. Deficiency can thus lead to neurotransmitter and neuropsychiatric disorders. The clinical spectrum of PTPSD is broad and differs according to age of onset, severity of disease, and whether preventative therapies were initiated and maintained from an early age. In the severe form, clinical symptoms may become apparent in the neonatal period and can include hypotonia, movement disorders, abnormal eye movements, autonomic dysregulation, and impaired development. Without treatment, developmental delays become more marked. Neurologic symptoms (dysarthria, dystonia, tremors, abnormal gait, parkinsonism, oculogyric crises, motor tics) may be ameliorated by treatment with sapropterin dihydrochloride and neurotransmitter precursors. Other features of the condition can include psychiatric comorbidities (ADHD, anxiety, depression), infant feeding difficulties leading to early growth failure, hyperprolactinemia, growth hormone deficiency, sleep issues, and autonomic dysfunction; many of these features can be ameliorated by appropriate treatment. In treated individuals, development often improves during adolescence, with many adults having a normal IQ level. In the mild (peripheral) form, affected individuals are usually asymptomatic apart from an increase in phenylalanine (Phe) levels. Some remain asymptomatic. However, with time, some have mild developmental delays and can develop deficiency of neurotransmitter production, such that treatment of some asymptomatic individuals may be required.Diagnosis/testingThe biochemical diagnosis of PTPSD is established in a proband with confirmed hyperphenylalaninemia, elevated neopterin levels, reduced biopterin levels, and a decreased biopterin-to-neopterin ratio in urine or dried blood spots (DBS) and normal dihydropteridine reductase (DHPR) activity in DBS. The molecular diagnosis of PTPSD is established in a proband by identification of biallelic pathogenic (or likely pathogenic) variants in PTS by molecular genetic testing.ManagementTargeted therapies: Immediate therapy with sapropterin (tetrahydrobiopterin dihydrochloride; BH4), a cofactor/cosubstrate of PAH, is recommended to reduce blood Phe concentrations in individuals with hyperphenylalaninemia. If sapropterin is not available, dietary Phe restriction should be implemented. Because sapropterin has limited access to the central nervous system (CNS), or rather, this access is only achieved at high doses, therapy with sapropterin does not normalize the activity of tyrosine or tryptophan hydroxylase in people with PTPSD. Additional treatment strategies are necessary for long-term management and may include the use of neurotransmitter precursors (levodopa plus decarboxylase inhibitor (DCI), i.e., carbidopa or benserazide), 5-hydroxytryptophan, and/or dopamine (rotigotine patch, pramipexole) and/or serotonin agonists, or other medications (MAO inhibitors such as selegiline) to address specific neurotransmitter deficiencies and maintain optimal neurologic function. Supportive care: Optimization of dosage and intervals of levodopa/DCI in those with abnormal movements/parkinsonism; growth hormone supplementation and/or optimization of neurotransmitter precursor therapy for growth hormone deficiency; optimization of neurotransmitter precursor therapy for recurrent hyperthermia; anticholinergic treatment may be considered for hypersalivation; standard treatment for developmental delay, spasticity, epilepsy, sleep disorders, and decreased bone mineral density. Biochemical surveillance: Routine Phe monitoring in infants (age Genetic counselingPTPSD is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. If both parents are known to be heterozygous for a PTS pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of inheriting neither of the familial PTS pathogenic variants. Children born of one parent with PTPSD and one parent with two normal PTS alleles are obligate heterozygotes. If the mother is the affected parent, MPKU syndrome is a critical issue. Females with PTPSD should receive counseling regarding the teratogenic effects of elevated maternal plasma Phe concentration (i.e., MPKU syndrome) when they reach childbearing age. Once the PTS pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing for PTPSD are possible.

title: Fabry Disease
abstract: Clinical characteristicsFabry disease is the most common of the lysosomal storage disorders and results from deficient activity of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A (α-Gal A), leading to progressive lysosomal deposition of globotriaosylceramide and its derivatives in cells throughout the body. The classic form, occurring in males with less than 1% α-Gal A enzyme activity, usually has its onset in childhood or adolescence with periodic crises of severe pain in the extremities (acroparesthesia), the appearance of vascular cutaneous lesions (angiokeratomas), sweating abnormalities (anhidrosis, hypohidrosis, and rarely hyperhidrosis), characteristic corneal and lenticular opacities, and proteinuria. Gradual deterioration of kidney function to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) usually occurs in men in the third to fifth decade. In middle age, most males successfully treated for ESKD develop cardiac and/or cerebrovascular disease, a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Heterozygous females typically have milder symptoms at a later age of onset than males. Rarely, females may be relatively asymptomatic throughout a normal life span or may have symptoms as severe as those observed in males with the classic phenotype. In contrast, late-onset forms occur in males with greater than 1% α-Gal A activity. Clinical manifestations include cardiac disease, which usually presents in the sixth to eighth decade with left ventricular hypertrophy, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, and proteinuria; kidney failure, associated with ESKD but without the skin lesions or pain; or cerebrovascular disease presenting as stroke or transient ischemic attack.Diagnosis/testingIdentification of deficient α-Gal A enzyme activity in plasma, isolated leukocytes, and/or cultured cells is the most efficient and reliable method of diagnosing Fabry disease in males. Identification of a hemizygous GLA pathogenic variant by molecular genetic testing confirms the diagnosis in a male proband. Identification of a heterozygous GLA pathogenic variant by molecular genetic testing establishes the diagnosis in a heterozygous female.ManagementTargeted therapies: Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with or without chaperone therapy (e.g., migalastat) to prevent and/or delay the progression of renal, cardiac, and cerebrovascular manifestations. Experts recommend that ERT be initiated as early as possible in all males with Fabry disease (including children and those with ESKD undergoing dialysis and kidney transplantation) and in females with clinical disease manifestations, as all are at high risk for renal, cardiac, and cerebrovascular complications. Supportive care: Diphenylhydantoin, carbamazepine, or gabapentin to reduce pain (acroparesthesia); aspirin, lipid-lowering agents, and blood pressure control for cardiac ischemia; aspirin and/or other antiplatelet agents may be recommended for stroke prophylaxis; ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers to reduce proteinuria; chronic hemodialysis and/or kidney transplantation for ESKD; rehabilitation and hearing aids for auditory and vestibular symptoms; management of psychiatric manifestations per psychologist. Surveillance: Annual assessment for angiokeratomas, acroparesthesia, sweating abnormalities, and gastrointestinal, pulmonary, and vascular manifestations; annual cardiology assessment with EKG and echocardiogram as recommended by cardiologist from age 18 years in males, biannual cardiology assessments in females from age 18 years; annual neurologic assessment with brain MRI\MRA every two to three years beginning at age 18 years; assessment of renal function including blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and urinalysis annually or more frequently as needed; annual audiology evaluations in males beginning at age 18 years and biannually in females; psychological assessment beginning at age 18 years annually or more frequently as needed. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Smoking. Amiodarone may or may not have detrimental effects in individuals with Fabry disease; evidence is insufficient. Evaluation of relatives at risk: Early identification of affected male and female relatives by molecular genetic testing (if the GLA pathogenic variant in the family is known) or, in males only, measurement of α-Gal A enzyme activity (if the GLA pathogenic variant in the family is not known) in order to initiate appropriate management as early as possible in affected individuals.Genetic counselingFabry disease is inherited in an X-linked manner: hemizygous males are affected; heterozygous females may be as severely affected as males or asymptomatic throughout a normal life span. In a family with more than one affected individual, the mother of an affected male is an obligate heterozygote. If a male is the only affected family member, his mother is likely heterozygous for the GLA pathogenic variant; rarely, a single affected male in a family may have a de novo pathogenic variant. A heterozygous female has a 50% chance of transmitting the GLA pathogenic variant in each pregnancy. An affected male transmits the pathogenic variant to all his daughters and none of his sons. Once the GLA pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, molecular genetic testing for at-risk relatives, prenatal testing for a pregnancy at increased risk, and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
